note: Single-pass extraction by Claude reading the paper text; evidence references sections/figures/tables. No multi-run validation.

components.description: LoRA's expressiveness/stability limits motivate GORP's low-rank gradient subspace design and its evidence

nodes.name: LoRA constrains expressiveness
nodes.description: LoRA's low-rank matrices constrain the parameter space and expressiveness, giving suboptimal performance versus full fine-tuning, with a gap that often widens in continual learning.

nodes.name: Explicit constraints are limited
nodes.description: Methods imposing explicit constraints on LoRA parameters (O-LoRA, MIGU, N-LoRA) can only approximate the ideal parameter space, cannot adapt to dynamically evolving gradient spaces, and struggle to capture shared features across tasks.

nodes.name: Gradients are low-rank
nodes.description: Gradients tend to adopt a low-rank structure during training, so full-rank parameter gradients can be projected into a low-rank space while keeping efficiency.

nodes.name: Moment-based gradient subspace
nodes.description: GORP builds the gradient shared space from Adam's first-order moment (SVD plus a k-rank approximation under threshold epsilon), since sampled hidden features may not represent the overall gradient direction.

nodes.name: Orthogonal subspace update across tasks
nodes.description: For tasks 2..T, GORP takes the part of the first-order moment orthogonal to the existing space, applies SVD/k-rank approximation, appends new vectors, and truncates small singular values to keep the space fixed in size.

nodes.name: GORP combines full and LoRA parameters
nodes.description: GORP trains both LoRA and full-rank parameters in a unified low-rank gradient subspace: LoRA parameter A's gradient is projected away from the old-task space, and full-rank gradients are updated in low-rank form.

nodes.name: GORP beats baselines on CL benchmarks
nodes.description: With T5-Large GORP gets Table 2 averages of 79.8 (standard CL) and 76.0 (large number of tasks), above O-LoRA, MIGU and N-LoRA, about 4% and 6.1% over baselines and near MTL; on LLaMA2-7B it reaches 78.6 (+2.5%).

nodes.name: GORP forgets far less
nodes.description: GORP's forgetting rate (BWT) is 0.8% versus 7.8% for the baseline, a 7.0% reduction on T5 standard CL benchmarks.

nodes.name: Stable gradient orthogonality
nodes.description: GORP keeps gradient orthogonality stable across tasks (Fig 2) while parameter orthogonality is only slightly weaker than the baseline (Fig 5), giving better gradient direction control with larger parameter freedom.

nodes.name: Better generalization to unseen tasks
nodes.description: On unseen tasks GORP improves average performance over N-LoRA by 7.0% and over O-LoRA by 26.2% across task orders.

nodes.name: Each component helps
nodes.description: Ablation shows low-rank projection on LoRA adds 0.7% over baseline, adding full-rank parameters with projection gives 2.0%, and the full GORP reaches 3.9%.

nodes.name: Efficient compared with O-LoRA
nodes.description: GORP needs nearly the same time as O-LoRA (0.99x) but far fewer FLOPs (about 1.8e-3x), whereas N-LoRA is faster but costs 1.23x FLOPs.

isolated_nodes.name: Task growth limitation
isolated_nodes.description: As task sequences grow, capturing increasing task diversity in the fixed-size gradient subspace is a key challenge, and effectiveness in complex real-world scenarios remains unvalidated.

structural_reasoning: Argument runs from LoRA and explicit-constraint limitations through GORP's gradient-subspace construction and projection to the empirical results.
